title: No conditions for life: Women, girls and the gendered dimensions of Israel’s genocide against Palestinians in Gaza – Report Launch, 25 November 2026 – Introductory Speech
content:
Dear colleagues and friends,

Thank you for joining us from around the world for the launch of our latest report on Gaza, No conditions for life: Women, girls and the gendered dimensions of Israel’s genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, which comes two years after we concluded unequivocally that Israel was committing genocide against Palestinians in the occupied Gaza Strip.

Thank you to all the Media present and others, for listening and reporting on the senseless killings and the victims, on how Palestinian organizations, Amnesty and other international organizations, the Special Rapporteur and the UN Commission of Inquiry and others have bravely urged the international community to protect Palestinians in Gaza from genocide and those in the West Bank from ethnic cleansing, despite the sanctions imposed on some, the threats on others, along with the propaganda and vicious silencing. 

-I-

It’s two years since Amnesty found that after October 2023, Israel had committed three of the five acts prohibited under the Genocide Convention a with the clear intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza.

title: Philippines: Duterte trial a defining test for justice, accountability and future of the ICC
content:
Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte’s trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) for crimes against humanity is a historic opportunity for justice for victims of the so-called “war on drugs” and a defining test for the future of international accountability, Amnesty International said ahead of the trial starting on Monday 30 November.

The trial, which will focus on murders and attempted murders allegedly committed between 2013 and 2019 while Duterte was President of the Philippines and Mayor of Davao City, opens at a time when the ICC is facing unprecedented attacks from the US government and other powerful states.

“For thousands of families of victims, this trial represents something they have been denied for years: the chance to see those allegedly responsible for horrific crimes brought before a court of law,” said Ritz Lee Santos III, Executive Director of Amnesty International Philippines.

“The victims and survivors of the so-called ‘war on drugs’ have shown extraordinary courage and determination in pursuing justice. They must remain at the centre of these proceedings every step of the way.”

title: Sri Lanka: UN report underscores need to end decades-long impunity for conflict-related crimes
content:
Responding to the publication of a new report by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) on crimes under international law committed during Sri Lanka’s 25-year internal armed conflict, Smriti Singh, Amnesty International’s South Asia Director, said:  

“This report shines a light on the fact that no progress has been made in addressing crimes under international law in Sri Lanka and that truth, justice and reparation remain elusive for hundreds and thousands of victims. Its findings reflect the unwillingness of successive Sri Lankan governments to investigate allegations and ensure accountability for abuses committed during the internal armed conflict that ended in 2009. Impunity persists even as mass graves continue to be identified, such as in Chemmani where recent exhumations found the remains of more than 583 individuals, including children.

title: Andorra: Long-awaited bill should be strengthened to fully decriminalize and guarantee access to abortion
content:
Ahead of an expected vote on a bill aimed at reforming Andorra’s legal framework on abortion, Amnesty International has published a statement calling for the bill to be strengthened and abortion fully decriminalized. Amnesty International’s Senior Campaigner, Monica Costa Riba said: 

“Andorra is the only country in Europe with a total ban on abortion. The bill is a step in the right direction by removing archaic criminal penalties for seeking healthcare. But lawmakers are missing an historic opportunity to guarantee safe abortion care if they keep criminal punishments for health professionals who perform them, making delivery of safe abortion care in the country impossible.

title: Indonesia: One year after devastating Aceh floods, communities face renewed flood risk as recovery stalls
content:
One year after catastrophic floods and landslides devastated Indonesia’s Aceh province, many survivors remain without adequate housing, continue to struggle to access promised support and now face renewed flood risks from this year’s rainy season, Amnesty International said in new research published today.

Amnesty’s briefing, A Continuing Crisis, found that many communities affected by the November 2025 disaster are still living with the consequences of inadequate response and recovery efforts. Many families remain in temporary shelters, damaged homes and makeshift accommodation, while reconstruction has progressed slowly and many survivors remain uncertain about what support they are entitled to receive.

“For the survivors in Aceh, this disaster did not end when the floodwaters receded. A year later, many families are still waiting for the housing and support they were promised by the Indonesian authorities,” said Montse Ferrer, Co-Regional Director at Amnesty International.

title: “I have never gotten used to the news”: Duaa Dhainy’s campaigning to halt Saudi Arabia’s executions and save lives
content:
More than 10 years ago, I began working with the European Saudi Organization for Human Rights, an organization founded by activists living in exile. Some had only recently fled Saudi Arabia to build new lives abroad, free from the fear of arrest and torture. Yet what they left behind continued to haunt them: friends in prison, families waiting for their children to be released, and fears for those still there. I would listen to my director, Ali al-Dubaisi, speaking about events in Saudi Arabia. Only later did I learn about the difficult journey he and his family had made into exile. I could see the responsibility he felt towards those who remained in Saudi Arabia, and how he turned it into daily work documenting violations and ensuring their voices were heard.

Over time, I realized that what I had first heard was only a fraction of what we would discover.

title: “I wish they could pass the bill today”: Ghanaian women accused of being witches on long-awaited legislation
content:
In Ghana, people accused of witchcraft, primarily older women, face threats, physical attacks and in some cases, death. They have no safe place to escape to other than camps in Northern and North-eastern regions overseen by religious leaders, as documented in Amnesty International’s 2025 report.

In 2023, the Anti-Witchcraft Accusations Bill, which seeks to establish a legal framework for addressing accusations of witchcraft and related abuses, including the protection and reintegration of persons affected, was passed by parliament as a private members’ bill. However, it was not signed into law by the then president, who cited constitutional concerns.  

In July 2026, the bill was reintroduced to Ghana’s Parliament as a private members bill. Since September, the government is moving to take over the bill as a government-sponsored bill, aiming to facilitate its passage and implementation. The Minister of Gender confirmed that government was working towards reintegration of camp residents and eventual closure of the camps.

Amnesty International visited three of these camps, in Gambaga, Kukuo and Gnani, in April and May 2026, where six resident women shared their stories and hopes.

title: Israel/OPT: Women and girls bear the crushing toll of Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza
content:
Israel has relentlessly inflicted repeated and cumulative harms on women and girls in the occupied Gaza Strip since October 2023 as an integral part of its ongoing genocide against Palestinians, said Amnesty International in a new report published today. 

No conditions for life: Women, girls and the gendered dimensions of Israel’s genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, lays out in 135 pages of harrowing detail, Israel’s ongoing genocide despite the so-called ceasefire of October 2025, providing evidence of how the Israeli military, between 7 October 2023 and 1 October 2026, has repeatedly killed, injured, forcibly displaced, unlawfully detained, deliberately denied women and girls access to essential healthcare, including reproductive healthcare, and starved them. It illustrates how these measures have forced women into a daily struggle for survival defined by grief and trauma and stripped away the conditions necessary for women to exercise autonomy over decisions relating to pregnancy, childbirth and reproductive health.

title: Europe: Judgments on ‘instrumentalization’ of migration a devastating blow to the absolute prohibition of torture
content:
Today, the European Court of Human Rights ruled on cases of summary forced returns at the borders of Latvia, Lithuania and Poland with Belarus, also known as pushbacks, in cases of “instrumentalization of migration” defined by the Court as the actions of a state encouraging, facilitating or forcing migration with the aim of destabilizing another state.

The Court found that summary returns at the border in this context constitute a violation of the prohibition of torture only where applicants showed “evident personal vulnerabilities” or were able to demonstrate a real and immediate threat to life or risk of ill-treatment. Reacting to the judgments, Mandi Mudarikwa, Head of Strategic Litigation at Amnesty International said:

“These rulings strike a devastating blow to legal certainty and the protection of human rights at the borders under the European Convention of Human Rights. They limit the absolute protections guaranteed under the Convention only to people who are able to show evident vulnerabilities or that they are at immediate risk. This is despite the Convention entrenching such rights, such as the prohibition of torture, as absolute and the Court itself recognizing this fact.

title: Egypt: Authorities must reverse decision to close Mada Masr and drop all charges against its editor in chief Lina Attalah
content:
Ahead of an appeal hearing on 25 November against the closure of Mada Masr and the conviction of its editor-in-chief Lina Attalah for operating a website without a license Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa, Sara Hashash, said:

“Egyptian authorities have an opportunity to change course and meet their international obligations by reversing this disgraceful decision to shut down Mada Masr. The latest escalation against Mada Masr is a chilling signal of the Egyptian authorities’ resolve to silence independent journalism and eradicate any critical reporting that challenges the official narrative or scrutinizes their human rights record or other conduct. Egyptian authorities must immediately end their brazen assault on press freedom, quash the closure order against Mada Masr– one of the few remaining lifelines for independent information about Egypt.

“The authorities should also drop all charges against Lina Attalah who faces trial in a separate case, on charges of publishing false news and operating a website without a licence, for which she could be sentenced to up to one year in prison.

title: Ethiopia: Lethal artillery strikes on civilian neighbourhoods in Tigray’s Alamata city must be investigated as war crimes
content:
Artillery attacks by Ethiopia’s military and its allied Tigray Peace Forces (TPF) that killed dozens of civilians and injured many more in the city of Alamata in the northern region of Tigray, between 26 and 28 September, must be investigated as possible war crimes, Amnesty International said today.

The organization also found that forces affiliated to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), put civilians in harm’s way by establishing military bases in populated residential areas, including in several schools in Alamata, prior to the outbreak of renewed fighting in the region.

The Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF) and its TPF allies seized control of the strategic city of Alamata, a key supply hub for troops, food, and fuel, from the TPLF on 28 September.

title: Bangladesh: Proposed changes to cyber laws risk granting authorities excessive power to police online content
content:
New proposed amendments to Bangladesh’s laws on online speech would give authorities wide-ranging and arbitrary powers to police content and restrict the right to freedom of expression, Amnesty International said today.

The new draft Cyber Protection (Amendment) Act, 2026 would grant government agencies overly broad powers to remove, block, or relocate any online content deemed to fall within a range of broadly defined categories that do not constitute legitimate reasons to restrict the right to freedom of expression under international human rights law. These include content that “undermines” the integrity, dignity […] of the country”, or content that is “likely to create religious or communal hatred”. The lowering of the threshold for removal or blocking to content which ‘is likely to’ undermine security or create religious or communal hatred is vague and speculative.
